output.title: When demo theatre becomes a hidden workflow cost
output.body:
If you’ve already tried ChatGPT but haven’t wired it into a real workflow, the quiet cost of demo theatre is easy to miss. It feels productive to polish another demo or proof of concept. But for an owner-operator, that can turn into time spent proving something might work while the repetitive work still sits there.

The real cost is not the demo itself. It is the time not spent on one recurring workflow with a measurable output. In a small business, that might be repeated customer questions, manual data work, follow-ups, or invoice handling. If the work does not repeat, AI is probably not the right place to start. No drama there; the machine can wait.

Bareni’s diagnostic stays bounded. We look for one recurring workflow, check honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, define a fixed-price pilot with clear measures. Timings and scope are intended, not guarantees. There is no mandatory roadmap gate in the middle, though a separate AI Strategy & Roadmap exists for people who want strategy only.

We also keep scope discipline: high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work stays out, along with bulk cold-email automation, scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows, and requests that depend on unsupported compliance or security claims. That is current scope discipline, not a claim that such work can never be automated.

A practical next step is to ask yourself one question: do I have a single repeating workflow that could justify the effort because it takes about 5–10 hours a week, has a measurable output, and still keeps human approval on the risky part?
